cases.abstract: VoxPoser translates language-specified manipulation subtasks into spatial objectives, allowing motion planning to combine desired motions and avoidance constraints rather than relying on sequential action primitives. Language-model-generated programs query visual perception and assign values to three-dimensional locations for an end-effector, object, or object part; planners optimize trajectories against these maps and replan from observations without additional training. Across five real-world tabletop tasks, success reaches 88% in static scenes and 70% under disturbances, versus 24% and 0% for an LLM using simple primitives. This comparison supports spatially composed objectives as an executable alternative to direct primitive parameterization, including when observations change. Across 13 simulated tasks, category averages favor VoxPoser on seen and unseen instruction/attribute splits, although individual tasks sometimes favor baselines. For contact-rich tasks, synthesized trajectories additionally focus exploration near task-relevant interactions for online dynamics learning. On three simulated tasks, this raises success from 3.3-18.3% zero-shot to 80.0-91.7%, with mean interaction times below three minutes, whereas learning without priors exceeds 12 hours. Thus, trajectories insufficient for zero-shot completion can still guide adaptation; perception errors, restricted environment dynamics, and end-effector-only planning delimit the demonstrated scope.
cases.notes: The operative relation is spatial constraints becoming a joint planning objective, not merely code generation. Table 1 tests execution against primitive parameterization; Tables 2 and 4 bound generalization by aggregate gains and task-level exceptions. Sections 3.4 and 4.3 explain why unsuccessful zero-shot trajectories can still restrict exploration to useful interactions, with adaptation evidence confined to simulation. Kept perception, dynamics, and planning limits; did not infer an isolated causal benefit from the benchmark comparisons.

cases.abstract: Similar training losses can conceal different generalization performance, so Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) targets low loss throughout a parameter neighborhood. A conditional PAC-Bayesian bound motivates worst-case neighborhood-loss minimization, assuming Gaussian perturbations do not reduce population loss and weight norm is at least one. The practical optimizer constructs a loss-increasing perturbation from one gradient, then updates the original weights using a second gradient at the perturbed weights. CIFAR models trained from scratch improve across all tested configurations despite non-SAM baselines being allowed twice as many epochs: AutoAugment WideResNet CIFAR-10 error falls from 2.2% to 1.6%. Gains on ImageNet ResNets and EfficientNet finetuning after ImageNet or ImageNet-plus-JFT pretraining extend this evidence beyond one training regime. Lower Hessian curvature in the tested model supports the intended neighborhood geometry, without establishing a generalization guarantee for approximate updates. With random label noise, SAM improves clean-test accuracy over SGD but trails MentorMix without bootstrapping; an augmented SVHN configuration also worsens. A complementary m-sharpness analysis maximizes loss separately over data subsets: smaller subsets tend to improve generalization and better predict generalization gaps in the evaluated settings, making subset size consequential rather than an implementation detail.
cases.notes: Section 2 links neighborhood loss to population-loss control only under the stated assumptions; the two-gradient approximation is not the theorem. Table 1 asks whether gains survive longer baseline training, while Tables 2-3 cover training from scratch and pretrained finetuning. Section 4.2 tests the targeted geometry, not its causal sufficiency for generalization. Section 4.1 makes independent subset maximizations recoverable as the co-contribution. Retained Table 4's MentorMix comparison and Table 5's SVHN exception.
